To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) humans can use machine learning interpretations to make better decisions than they could without them, (2) humans can use these interpretations to improve their own performance in a cooperative game with a machine, and (3) the effectiveness of interpretations depends on the user's expertise and the quality of the interpretation.

(1) the interpretation that provides the most information to human users is also the most helpful, (2) human users are more likely to accept a prediction from the computer that includes an interpretation, and (3) human users are less likely to accept the computer’s prediction when they have to choose between two interpretations.

1) humans can benefit from machine interpretations, but only in the case of novices and when the interpretation is in a natural language; 2) humans prefer to have more information, and 3) humans are not good at understanding the model’s uncertainty, but can learn to understand the uncertainty by interacting with the model.

how to evaluate interpretations in real-world settings, and how to design better human-in-the-loop systems.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the best interpretations do not necessarily have to be the most human-interpretable, but rather the ones that are the most useful for the task.

the effectiveness of interpretation depends on the user's domain expertise and task difficulty, and that interpretation is most effective in improving user's decision making when it is provided as a recommendation.
the best interpretation method for human-in-the-loop is to provide a confidence score, which is a simple and effective way to improve human performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effectiveness of interpretations depends on the user’s prior knowledge and the user’s task.
interpretation is effective in improving human performance when it is (i) grounded, i.e., it provides a reason for the prediction, and (ii) informative, i.e., the reason is not trivial.
interpretation can improve human decision making in cooperative settings, and that the choice of interpretation is crucial to the quality of the human-machine interaction.
